title: Shari'ah and fiqh
hookLine: shari'ah is the path Allah set; fiqh is the scholars' understanding of it

cards: Two words get used as if they meant the same thing, in headlines and arguments and around dinner tables. Shari'ah. Fiqh.
Inside the tradition they aren't the same, and the space between them is where this whole new block lives. One is the path Allah set.
The other is the scholars' understanding of that path: written down, argued over, refined, sometimes corrected. A path, and maps of it drawn by careful people.
A new block begins today, on fiqh and the schools of law, and it starts by telling the two apart. Today: shari'ah.

teach.b: First, shari'ah. The word is in the Qur'an itself. In surah al-Jathiyah, Allah tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that He has set him on a shari'ah, a clear road of the command, and tells him to follow it.
So the word names something Allah sets, not something people invent.

Second, fiqh, which means understanding. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says that when Allah wants good for someone, He gives that person understanding of the religion, and the verb there is the verb of fiqh.

Fiqh is the scholars' work: reading the Qur'an and the sunnah closely and working out what they ask of a person in prayer, fasting, trade, marriage and the rest of a life. Third, why the difference matters.
Muslims hold the shari'ah to come from Allah. Fiqh is human understanding of it, and a scholar can be right or wrong.

Bukhari records the Prophet saying that a judge who strives for the right ruling and reaches it has two rewards, and one who strives and misses has one. An honest error, after real effort, is still rewarded.
That's part of why there are schools of law, and why their differences can stand side by side. Fourth, the picture.

teach.h: THE MAP IS NOT THE LAND.
teach.b: A map is drawn from the land by people who walked it carefully. Good maps can differ in what they show and how. None of them is the land itself.
Sunni and Shia scholars both draw these maps, each with their own methods, and this block looks next at the sources they draw from, beginning tomorrow with the Qur'an.

how: Muslims who want to know how to pray, fast or trade rightly turn to fiqh, the rulings scholars have worked out, often through the books or teachers of one school of law.

o: a set of punishments a government enforces by law
the path Allah set, as distinct from scholars' understanding
the detailed rulings scholars wrote in their law books

games.q: shari'ah and fiqh — tap the pairs.
p: a judge who strives and is right
a judge who strives and misses

s: shari'ah and fiqh are two words for the same thing
shari'ah is the path Allah set; fiqh is the scholars' understanding of it.
the word shari'ah appears in the Qur'an
in surah al-Jathiyah, Allah sets the Prophet on a shari'ah and tells him to follow it.
a scholar who strives and gets it wrong earns nothing
Bukhari records one reward for an honest miss, and two for getting it right.

games.q: you're a judge. you've studied the case and the texts with real care, and you're still not certain. what does the hadith in Bukhari say?
o: never rule until you're certain you're right.
strive and rule; an honest error after real effort still earns a reward.
games.why: strive and get it right, two rewards; strive and miss, one. the effort is honored, which is part of why schools can differ with respect.

practice: Say the two words slowly, one on each breath: shari'ah, the path; fiqh, the understanding, the map.
Then take one ordinary act from your day, washing, eating, a kind word, and notice its two layers: the good it aims at, and the careful how-to people have worked out.
